stimulus.source_note: Photograph: graffiti painted during the occupation of Alcatraz Island (National Park Service photograph, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons); the photograph was viewed before writing. Account drawn from the grounding books and verified against the National Park Service and HISTORY timelines: occupation began November 20, 1969; the island was a former federal prison closed in 1963; the occupation ended June 11, 1971.
stimulus.text:
The photograph shows a wall on Alcatraz Island painted with the words "WELCOME" and "INDIAN LAND." A sign on the wall reads "UNITED INDIAN PROPERTY."

On November 20, 1969, a group of activists calling themselves Indians of All Tribes landed on Alcatraz Island, a former federal prison in San Francisco Bay that the government had closed in 1963. They claimed the island by right of discovery and said they would build an Indian school, cultural center, and museum there. The occupation lasted until June 1971.

stem: The Alcatraz occupation is best understood as significant mainly because it

options.text: won the island for the occupiers, who still govern it today
options.misconception: The passage says the occupation lasted until June 1971; the occupiers did not keep the island.

options.text: drew national attention to Indian grievances and inspired further Native activism
ended the Bureau of Indian Affairs and restored all broken treaties
options.misconception: The Bureau of Indian Affairs was not ended, and the treaties were not restored.

options.text: proved that occupations always win their demands from the federal government
options.misconception: The occupiers did not win the island, so the occupation does not prove that occupations always win.

rationales.A: The passage says the occupation ended in June 1971; the occupiers did not keep the island.
rationales.B: Background from the books: The occupation made national headlines for nineteen months and inspired later actions, including the Trail of Broken Treaties in 1972 and Wounded Knee in 1973.
rationales.C: Background: The Bureau of Indian Affairs was not ended, and the broken treaties were not restored.
rationales.D: The occupiers did not win the island, so the occupation cannot prove that occupations always win.
rationales.general:
1. The occupation lasted from November 1969 until June 1971, far longer than a one-day protest.
2. Background: That long, visible occupation put Indian grievances on national television and in newspapers.
3. Background: It inspired later Native actions, including the Trail of Broken Treaties in 1972 and the Wounded Knee occupation in 1973.
4. Its importance lies in that attention and inspiration, not in keeping the island.
Remember: A protest can fail to win its stated demand and still change what the country talks about.
